definition: The zodiac degree rising on the eastern horizon at your moment of birth. It anchors the chart's orientation and is central to determining the houses, which is why an accurate birth time matters so much.

A meaningful geometric angle between two planets or points in a chart. Astrologers use aspects to consider how those functions relate, but the planets involved, their condition, the houses, the orb, and the rest of the chart all shape the interpretation.

A map of the sky calculated for the date, time, and place of your birth. It supplies astronomical positions; astrology is the interpretive practice of considering how those positions may relate to one another and to a lived life.
Shorthand for your Sun sign, Moon sign, and rising sign, three placements people often learn first. They offer useful orientation, but they are only part of a much larger chart.
Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn, the signs that begin each season. In astrological symbolism, cardinal signs are associated with initiation and setting things in motion.
A chart created from mathematical midpoints between two people's charts and interpreted as a symbolic picture of the relationship as a whole rather than either person separately.

An aspect of 0°, placing two planets at or near the same zodiacal degree. Their functions are interpreted together, with the character of the conjunction depending heavily on the planets involved and the rest of the chart.

A boundary or starting degree, most often referring to the beginning of a house. In popular language, 'born on the cusp' means a birthday near a sign change, though the Sun occupies one zodiacal degree and therefore one sign at any given moment.
The zodiac is a 360° circle divided into twelve 30° signs. A planet's degree pinpoints its position within a sign, for example 9°40′ Pisces.
The point opposite the Ascendant on the western horizon. It is associated with the relationship axis and, in many house systems, marks the beginning of the seventh house.

A solar or lunar alignment that occurs near the Moon's nodes: a solar eclipse at a new moon and a lunar eclipse at a full moon. Astrologers give eclipses special interpretive weight, though how strongly one matters personally depends on its relationship to an individual chart.
One of four groupings of the signs: Fire, Earth, Air, and Water. Each element contains three signs and describes one layer of astrological temperament and style.
A table of planetary positions over time, used to determine where celestial bodies were, are, or will be by zodiacal degree.
Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius, the signs at the middle of each season. In astrological symbolism, fixed signs are associated with sustaining, concentrating, and maintaining.

The Moon opposite the Sun, when the lunar disk appears fully illuminated from Earth. Astrologically, full moons are often interpreted as points of visibility, culmination, or heightened awareness within a lunar cycle.
The written symbol used for a planet, sign, point, or aspect: part of the visual shorthand of an astrology chart.

A branch of astrology that addresses a specific question using a chart cast for the time the question is received and understood by the astrologer. It does not require the querent's birth data. Mo holds a Practitioner's Certificate in Horary Astrology from the School of Traditional Astrology.

One of twelve divisions of a horoscope used to organize areas of experience. A planet's house position adds context for where its themes may be expressed, and house placement depends on birth time and the house system being used.

A method for dividing a chart into houses, such as Placidus, whole sign, equal, Regiomontanus, and others. Different systems can place the same planet in different houses, so the method matters to interpretation.
A planet's entry into a new zodiac sign. Astrologers interpret an ingress as a change in the sign context through which that planet's symbolism is being expressed.
The Sun and Moon, traditionally called the two lights. Astrology commonly groups them with the planets for interpretive convenience even though neither is a planet astronomically.
A lunar cycle from one new moon to the next, about 29.5 days. The word is also commonly used for a particular new moon or full moon.

The point where the ecliptic intersects the local meridian above the horizon. Astrologically it is associated with public direction, reputation, visibility, and vocation; depending on the house system, it does not always equal the tenth-house cusp.
One of three ways the signs are grouped by seasonal position and symbolic mode of action: cardinal (initiating), fixed (sustaining), and mutable (adapting).
Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces, the signs that close each season. In astrological symbolism, mutable signs are associated with adapting, distributing, and transitioning.
Belonging to the birth chart. A natal Mars in Leo, for example, refers to Mars's position at birth, as distinct from Mars's current position by transit.

The conjunction of the Sun and Moon as seen from Earth, when the Moon is not visibly illuminated. Astrologically it is often treated as the opening of a new lunar cycle rather than as a command to begin something.

The two points where the Moon's orbital path crosses the ecliptic. In astrology they are interpreted as an axis, with different traditions assigning different meanings to the North and South Nodes. Eclipses occur near them.

The allowance, measured in degrees, within which an aspect is treated as active. Astrologers use different orb limits depending on the planets, aspect, technique, and school; tighter aspects are generally given more weight.

The apparent backward motion of a planet from Earth's viewpoint, produced by orbital geometry rather than an actual reversal in space. Astrologers interpret retrogrades in different ways, often giving added attention to review, reconsideration, internalization, or repetition of that planet's themes.
Everyday name for the Ascendant: the zodiac sign rising in the east at the moment of birth.

An astrological relationship assigning planets to signs they are said to rule. Rulership is used to connect parts of a chart through the condition and placement of the ruling planet; different traditions may use traditional or modern rulership schemes.
A traditional astrological distinction between day and night charts. It changes how some traditional techniques assess planetary condition, particularly the benefics and malefics.
One of twelve 30° divisions of the zodiac. In astrology, the sign provides one layer of context for how a planet or point may express; it does not operate independently from the rest of the chart.

A chart cast for the moment each year when the transiting Sun returns to the exact zodiacal degree of the natal Sun. Astrologers use it as one timing technique for considering themes and conditions of the year ahead.

The apparent slowing and stopping of a planet before it changes apparent direction, either retrograde or direct. Astrologers often give a station additional interpretive emphasis, though how much weight it receives depends on the technique and context.
A relationship-astrology technique that compares two charts, especially the aspects and house contacts between them, to explore how the two sets of chart factors interact.
The current position and movement of a planet, especially when compared with a natal chart. Transits are one way astrologers study timing, changing conditions, and the activation of natal placements.

A broad label for pre-modern Western astrological techniques and lineages, including methods involving sect, dignity, rulership, horary, and predictive judgment. Mo has studied and uses techniques from traditional astrology, but does not define her practice by a single school.
A 360° band divided into twelve signs along the ecliptic. Western tropical astrology anchors the zodiac to the equinoxes and solstices rather than to the changing positions of the constellations.
